content.narrative_summary: This page presents the first five of the Top 10 Take-Home Messages: 1) Treatment decisions for coronary revascularization should be based on clinical indications regardless of patient demographics. 2) When optimal strategy is unclear, a Heart Team approach with patient-centered, shared decision-making is recommended. 3) Surgical revascularization is indicated for significant left main disease, with percutaneous options reasonable for selected patients. 4) Contemporary trials support survival benefits of revascularization in stable ischemic heart disease with preserved ejection fraction and multivessel disease, though benefits of percutaneous revascularization remain uncertain. 5) The radial artery is preferred as a surgical conduit over other options.

content.narrative_summary: The page begins the PREAMBLE, noting that since 1980 the ACC and AHA have translated evidence into clinical practice guidelines using systematic methods. It outlines the guidelines’ intended use—to improve quality of care and inform clinical decisions—emphasizes the role of shared decision-making and patient engagement in implementation, and describes the ongoing methodology modernization by the Joint Committee to enhance user-friendliness, modular presentation, and cost-value analyses.

rows.recommendation: Radial artery access is recommended in patients undergoing percutaneous intervention who have acute coronary syndrome or stable ischemic heart disease, to reduce bleeding and vascular complications compared with a femoral approach. Patients with acute coronary syndrome also benefit from a reduction in mortality rate with this approach.

A short duration of dual antiplatelet therapy after percutaneous revascularization in patients with stable ischemic heart disease is reasonable to reduce the risk of bleeding events. After consideration of recurrent ischemia and bleeding risks, select patients may safely transition to P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy and stop aspirin after 1 to 3 months of dual antiplatelet therapy.

Staged percutaneous intervention (while in hospital or after discharge) of a significantly stenosed non-culprit artery in patients presenting with an ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction is recommended in select patients to improve outcomes. Percutaneous intervention of the nonculprit artery at the time of primary percutaneous coronary intervention is less clear and may be considered in stable patients with uncomplicated revascularization of the culprit artery, low-complexity nonculprit artery disease, and normal renal function. In contrast, percutaneous intervention of the non-culprit artery can be harmful in patients in cardiogenic shock.

Revascularization decisions in patients with diabetes and multivessel coronary artery disease are optimized by the use of a Heart Team approach. Patients with diabetes who have triple-vessel disease should undergo surgical revascularization; percutaneous coronary intervention may be considered if they are poor candidates for surgery.

Treatment decisions for patients undergoing surgical revascularization of coronary artery disease should include the calculation of a patient’s surgical risk with the Society of Thoracic Surgeons score. The usefulness of the SYNTAX score calculation in treatment decisions is less clear because of the interobserver variability in its calculation and its absence of clinical variables.

content.title: Improving Equity of Care in Revascularization and Shared Decision-Making
section_headings: 2. IMPROVING EQUITY OF CARE IN REVASCULARIZATION AND SHARED DECISION-MAKING
2.1 Improving Equity of Care in Revascularization
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis outlines that disparities in cardiovascular care and outcomes persist for women and non-White patients due to sociodemographic factors such as socioeconomic status, education, regional hospital quality, and insurance access. Observational studies and post hoc analyses of randomized trials show similar outcomes across racial and sex groups when treatment strategies are applied equally, indicating that inequities arise from differences in access and implementation of guideline-based therapies. Continuous efforts are needed to counter conscious and unconscious bias and ensure all patients receive appropriate care regardless of sex, race, or ethnicity.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation to Improve Equity of Care in Revascularization

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients who require coronary revascularization, treatment decisions should be based on clinical indication, regardless of sex (1-7) or race or ethnicity (8-10), and efforts to reduce disparities of care are warranted (11,12).

content.title: 2.2 Shared Decision-Making and Informed Consent
content.narrative_summary: The page defines shared decision-making as a collaborative, evidence-based dialogue between patients and clinicians that aligns treatment decisions with patient values and preferences. It emphasizes the importance of clear terminology, decision aids, and consideration of social determinants of health in patient engagement. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text outlines how shared decision-making improves patient understanding, sets realistic expectations, and enhances adherence and satisfaction, while identifying barriers such as low health literacy, cultural beliefs, language barriers, and comorbidities. It also describes the clinician’s responsibilities to present risks and benefits, include family consultation, and respect patient treatment preferences.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Shared Decision-Making and Informed Consent

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients undergoing revascularization, decisions should be patient centered—that is, considerate of the patient’s preferences and goals, cultural beliefs, health literacy, and social determinants of health—and made in collaboration with the patient’s support system (1,2).

2. In patients undergoing coronary angiography or revascularization, adequate information about benefits, risks, therapeutic consequences, and potential alternatives in the performance of percutaneous and surgical myocardial revascularization should be given, when feasible, with sufficient time for informed decision-making to improve clinical outcomes (3–5).

content.title: 4.3. Use of Coronary Physiology to Guide Revascularization With PCI
content.narrative_summary: Fractional flow reserve (FFR) and instantaneous wave-free ratio (iFR) are resting physiological indices used to assess the significance of coronary lesions, with FFR requiring maximal hyperemia and iFR measured during diastole. Randomized trials (including FAME 2) and observational studies have evaluated their impact on clinical endpoints such as death, myocardial infarction, and repeat revascularization. While FFR- and iFR-guided PCI reduces ischemia-driven interventions, further large randomized trials are needed to define their role, particularly in surgical revascularization.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the Use of Coronary Physiology to Guide Revascularization With PCI

rows.recommendation: In patients with angina or an anginal equivalent, undocumented ischemia, and angiographically intermediate stenoses, the use of fractional flow reserve (FFR) or instantaneous wave-free ratio (iFR) is recommended to guide the decision to proceed with PCI (1–6).
In stable patients with angiographically intermediate stenoses and FFR >0.80 or iFR >0.89, PCI should not be performed (7–10).

section_headings: 4.4 Intravascular Ultrasound to Assess Lesion Severity
5.1 Revascularization of the Infarct Artery in Patients With STEMI
content.narrative_summary: The page opens mid-discussion of the iFR-SWEDEHEART trials, reporting that patients deferred from PCI based on FFR >0.80 or iFR >0.89 experienced MACE rates of approximately 4.05% and 4.12%, with unplanned revascularization as the most frequent event, and notes that borderline values may warrant further ischemia testing. In the Synopsis, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) is described as providing superior anatomic detail beyond angiography, particularly for left main lesions, offering high spatial resolution (100–150 μm) and accurate lumen and plaque characterization correlated with physiologic indices. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text summarizes that deferral of intervention when IVUS shows a minimal lumen area ≥6 to 7.5 mm² is safe, with lower cutoffs (4.5–4.8 mm²) possibly appropriate in Asian patients; FFR and IVUS area cutoffs correlate in left main disease, and optical coherence tomography correlates with IVUS but is limited by blood clearance requirements for ostial lesions.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for Intravascular Ultrasound to Assess Lesion Severity

rows.recommendation: In patients with intermediate stenosis of the left main artery, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) is reasonable to help define lesion severity (1–5).

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis emphasizes that immediate reperfusion with primary PCI improves mortality in STEMI and is preferred over fibrinolysis except when PCI is not immediately available or expected delays exceed 120 minutes, with early transfer to PCI-capable centers; CABG has a limited acute role but advances in surgical technique and mechanical support may improve outcomes. The recommendation-specific supportive text summarizes multiple RCTs and meta-analyses showing primary PCI reduces death, MI, stroke, and bleeding compared with fibrinolysis, highlights early revascularization benefit in cardiogenic shock, discusses CABG and mechanical complication management in STEMI, and notes rescue PCI reduces cardiovascular events after failed fibrinolysis.

rows.recommendation: In patients with STEMI who are stable and presenting 12 to 24 hours after symptom onset, PCI is reasonable to improve clinical outcomes (21,22).

In patients with STEMI in whom PCI is not feasible or successful, with a large area of myocardium at risk, emergency or urgent CABG can be effective as a reperfusion modality to improve clinical outcomes (23,24).

In patients with STEMI complicated by ongoing ischemia, acute severe heart failure, or life-threatening arrhythmia, PCI can be beneficial to improve clinical outcomes, irrespective of time delay from MI onset.
In asymptomatic stable patients with STEMI who have a totally occluded infarct artery >24 hours after symptom onset and are without evidence of severe ischemia, PCI should not be performed (25,26).

In patients with STEMI, emergency CABG should not be performed after failed primary PCI:
• In the absence of ischemia or a large area of myocardium at risk, or
• If surgical revascularization is not feasible because of a no-reflow state or poor distal targets.

content.narrative_summary: The narrative discusses randomized trials of rescue PCI, highlighting higher bleeding and stroke risk with femoral access that can be mitigated by half-dose tenecteplase, radial access, and avoiding routine glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors. It notes reduced MACE with early routine angiography after fibrinolytic therapy, supported by meta-analyses showing decreased death or infarction with early invasive approaches. Early-transfer studies found that over 80% of transferred patients underwent PCI with significant improvement in residual stenosis, particularly when angiography occurred early after symptom onset or fibrinolytic administration. Finally, it comments on the limited evidence for PCI in asymptomatic patients presenting 12–24 hours after symptom onset, including the BRAVE-2 trial.

section_headings: 5.2. Revascularization of the Non-Infarct Artery in Patients With STEMI
content.narrative_summary: Paragraphs 7–10 continue discussion of management of STEMI patients beyond early presentation, noting limited RCT evidence for PCI in occluded or complex anatomy beyond 12–24 hours, situations where PCI may not be possible, potential harms of delayed or routine non-infarct artery PCI in cardiogenic shock, and consideration of emergency CABG when PCI fails or no-reflow occurs.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Revascularization of the Non-Infarct Artery in Patients With STEMI

rows.recommendation: In selected hemodynamically stable patients with STEMI and multivessel disease, after successful primary PCI, staged PCI of a significant non-infarct artery stenosis is recommended to reduce the risk of death or MI (1-4).
In selected patients with STEMI with complex multivessel non-infarct artery disease, after successful primary PCI, elective CABG is reasonable to reduce the risk of cardiac events.

In selected hemodynamically stable patients with STEMI and low-complexity multivessel disease, PCI of a non-infarct artery stenosis may be considered at the time of primary PCI to reduce cardiac event rates (1,2,5-7).

In patients with STEMI complicated by cardiogenic shock, routine PCI of a non-infarct artery at the time of primary PCI should not be performed because of the higher risk of death or renal failure (8-10).

content.title: 2021 ACC/AHA/SCAI Coronary Revascularization Guideline
content.narrative_summary: This page presents the Synopsis of the Heart Team approach to determine optimal revascularization in STEMI patients with multivessel CAD, outlining strategies including multivessel PCI, staged PCI of non-infarct arteries, ischemia-guided PCI, and elective CABG, and reviews trial evidence (RCTs, meta-analyses) supporting multivessel PCI safety and efficacy. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text summarizes key trial data: RCTs showing MACE reduction with staged PCI versus culprit-only PCI (COMPLETE trial), the role of physiologic testing (iFR/FFR), elective CABG after PCI for complex disease, MACE reduction with multivessel PCI at primary PCI (culprit artery-only vs multivessel strategies), and recommendation for culprit vessel-only primary PCI in STEMI with cardiogenic shock based on CULPRIT-SHOCK findings, with discussion of associated risks.

content.title: Figure 4. Revascularization of Noninfarct-Related Coronary Artery Lesions in Patients With STEMI
content.narrative_summary: Flowchart algorithm for management of non–infarct-related coronary lesions in STEMI patients following successful PCI of the infarct artery. The decision pathway considers cardiogenic shock, patient risk and lesion complexity, and presence of large-area myocardium at risk. Options include immediate or staged PCI of non-culprit artery(ies), routine deferment of non-culprit PCI in complex cases, Heart Team discussion, CABG, or GDMT. recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Coronary Angiography and Revascularization in Patients With NSTE-ACS

rows.recommendation: In patients with NSTE-ACS who are at elevated risk of recurrent ischemic events and are appropriate candidates for revascularization, an invasive strategy with the intent to proceed with revascularization is indicated to reduce cardiovascular events (1-4).

In appropriate patients with NSTE-ACS who have refractory angina or hemodynamic or electrical instability, an immediate invasive strategy with intent to perform revascularization is indicated to improve outcomes (10).

In patients with NSTE-ACS who are initially stabilized and are at high risk of clinical events, it is reasonable to choose an early invasive strategy (within 24 hours) over a delayed invasive strategy to improve outcomes (11-16).

In patients with NSTE-ACS who are initially stabilized and are at intermediate or low risk of clinical events, an invasive strategy with intent to perform revascularization is reasonable before hospital discharge to improve outcomes (11-16).

In patients with NSTE-ACS who have failed PCI and have ongoing ischemia, hemodynamic compromise, or threatened occlusion of an artery with substantial myocardium at risk, who are appropriate candidates for CABG, emergency CABG is reasonable (5-7,17).
In patients with NSTE-ACS who present in cardiogenic shock, routine multivessel PCI of non-culprit lesions in the same setting should not be performed (18,19).

content.title: 7. REVASCULARIZATION IN SIHD
section_headings: 7.1. Revascularization to Improve Survival in SIHD Compared With Medical Therapy
content.narrative_summary: Studies demonstrate that CABG confers a survival benefit over medical therapy in patients with SIHD, including those with left main CAD, triple-vessel CAD, and ischemic cardiomyopathy, although many of these trials predate modern antiplatelet, statin, beta-blocker, and ACE inhibitor/ARB therapies. There are no RCTs showing a survival advantage of PCI over medical therapy in SIHD, but PCI may be advantageous for patients with prohibitive surgical risk. The Heart Team should weigh the risks and benefits of PCI versus medical therapy in such patients.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Revascularization to Improve Survival in SIHD Compared With Medical Therapy

rows.recommendation: In patients with SIHD and multivessel CAD appropriate for CABG with severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction <35%), CABG is recommended to improve survival (1,2).

In selected patients with SIHD and multivessel CAD appropriate for CABG and mild-to-moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction 35%-50%), CABG (to include a left internal mammary artery [LIMA] graft to the LAD) is reasonable to improve survival (3-8).
In patients with SIHD and significant left main stenosis, CABG is recommended to improve survival (9-12).
In selected patients with SIHD and significant left main stenosis for whom PCI can provide equivalent revascularization to that possible with CABG, PCI is reasonable to improve survival (9).

In patients with SIHD, normal ejection fraction, significant stenosis in 3 major coronary arteries (with or without proximal LAD), and anatomy suitable for CABG, CABG may be reasonable to improve survival (10,13-15).

In patients with SIHD, normal ejection fraction, significant stenosis in 3 major coronary arteries (with or without proximal LAD), and anatomy suitable for PCI, the usefulness of PCI to improve survival is uncertain (14-24).

In patients with SIHD, normal left ventricular ejection fraction, and significant stenosis in the proximal LAD, the usefulness of coronary revascularization to improve survival is uncertain (10,14,17,24-27).

In patients with SIHD, normal left ventricular ejection fraction, and 1- or 2-vessel CAD not involving the proximal LAD, coronary revascularization is not recommended to improve survival (10,14,16,26,28,29).

In patients with SIHD who have ≥1 coronary arteries that are not anatomically or functionally significant (<70% diameter of non-left main coronary artery stenosis, FFR >0.80), coronary revascularization should not be performed with the primary or sole intent to improve survival (26,30).

The synopsis notes that while prior guidelines emphasized survival or ischemic symptom reduction with CABG or PCI versus medical therapy, other events such as cardiac death, myocardial infarction (MI), and urgent revascularization also influence prognosis. content.title: 7.3. Revascularization to Improve Symptoms
section_headings: 8. SITUATIONS IN WHICH PCI OR CABG WOULD BE PREFERRED
content.narrative_summary: The page provides two recommendation sections with supporting synopses. In the first, revascularization (PCI or CABG) is shown by multiple RCTs to improve anginal symptoms and quality of life more than optimal medical therapy, with durable benefit at 3 years post-procedure; trials include ORBITA and ISCHEMIA, and both PCI and CABG benefit patients with diabetes though CABG may yield greater intermediate-term health status. Inappropriate revascularization of nonobstructive lesions can worsen underlying CAD or cause periprocedural MI without symptom improvement. The second synopsis notes that CABG and PCI improve blood flow by different mechanisms—PCI treats focal obstructions while bypass grafts deliver blood beyond lesions—and that these differences inform strategy in patients with complex or diffuse CAD.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Revascularization to Improve Symptoms

rows.recommendation: In patients with refractory angina despite medical therapy and with significant coronary artery stenoses amenable to revascularization, revascularization is recommended to improve symptoms (1-6).
In patients with angina but no anatomic or physiological criteria for revascularization, neither CABG nor PCI should be performed (7,8).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Patients With Complex Disease

rows.recommendation: In patients who require revascularization for significant left main CAD with high-complexity CAD, it is recommended to choose CABG over PCI to improve survival (1,2).
In patients who require revascularization for multivessel CAD with complex or diffuse CAD (e.g., SYNTAX score >33), it is reasonable to choose CABG over PCI to confer a survival advantage (2-5).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Patients With Diabetes

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with diabetes and multivessel CAD with the involvement of the LAD, who are appropriate candidates for CABG, CABG (with a LIMA to the LAD) is recommended in preference to PCI to reduce mortality and repeat revascularizations (1-8).

2. In patients with diabetes who have multivessel CAD amenable to PCI and an indication for revascularization and are poor candidates for surgery, PCI can be useful to reduce long-term ischemic outcomes (9,10).

3. In patients with diabetes who have left main stenosis and low- or intermediate-complexity CAD in the rest of the coronary anatomy, PCI may be considered an alternative to CABG to reduce major adverse cardiovascular outcomes (5,11).

In patients with previous CABG and complex CAD, it may be reasonable to choose CABG over PCI when an IMA can be used as a conduit to the LAD (3,4).

content.title: 10.3 Use of Intravascular Imaging
content.narrative_summary: Intracoronary imaging (IVUS and OCT) overcomes angiographic limitations by providing detailed vessel visualization for stent sizing and post-PCI assessment. IVUS offers full-thickness vessel wall views to guide lesion preparation and detect complications, while OCT yields high-resolution images useful for assessing plaque morphology and stent apposition but requires blood clearance and has limited depth. Multiple randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrate that IVUS-guided PCI reduces major adverse cardiovascular events and target-vessel failure compared with angiography guidance. OCT-guided PCI is noninferior to IVUS in stent area outcomes and shows potential for improved physiologic results, with minimum stent area thresholds predicting MACE.

rows.recommendation: In patients undergoing coronary stent implantation, IVUS can be useful for procedural guidance, particularly in cases of left main or complex coronary artery stenting, to reduce ischemic events (1-10).
In patients undergoing coronary stent implantation, OCT is a reasonable alternative to IVUS for procedural guidance, except in ostial left main disease (11-13).
In patients with stent failure, IVUS or OCT is reasonable to determine the mechanism of stent failure (14-17).

content.title: Treatment of CTO
content.narrative_summary: Chronic total occlusion (CTO) occurs in about one-quarter of coronary angiography patients. Advances have yielded >80% procedural success, but 30-day mortality is 1.3% and perforation 4.8%. Retrospective data suggested improved outcomes with successful recanalization, but randomized trials have not shown functional or symptomatic benefit. Shared decision-making is recommended. Registry and retrospective data suggest potential benefit, but prospective randomized trials (EXPLORE, REVASC, EURO CTO) have not demonstrated improvement in ventricular function or symptoms with CTO PCI compared to medical therapy.

section_headings: 10.8. Treatment of Patients With Stent Restenosis
content.narrative_summary: The page begins by discussing that Optimal Medical Therapy versus CTO PCI trials yielded mixed results with no difference in symptoms or outcomes, noting that future trials may change the landscape. The Synopsis highlights that newer-generation drug-eluting stents (DES) significantly reduce in-stent restenosis (ISR) and target-lesion revascularization compared to bare-metal stents and first-generation DES, with ISR occurring in 5–10% of patients post-PCI driven by neointimal hyperplasia. Various treatment modalities—including balloon angioplasty, DES, drug-coated balloons, vascular brachytherapy, atherectomy, and CABG—are explored, with DES providing the greatest benefit; treatment should be individualized based on ISR type and lesion characteristics, and intensive medical therapy remains vital. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text summarizes evidence: DES lower target-vessel restenosis rates compared to BMS or angioplasty, everolimus-eluting stents having the best efficacy without significant differences in death or MI; CABG may be preferred for diffuse or complex ISR such as CTO with multivessel disease; and vascular brachytherapy offers an option for recurrent ISR in patients unsuitable for further stenting or bypass.

In patients who develop recurrent ISR, brachytherapy may be considered to improve symptoms (5).

content.title: 10.9. Hemodynamic Support for Complex PCI
section_headings: 11.1. Aspirin and Oral P2Y12 Inhibitors in Patients Undergoing PCI
content.narrative_summary: Patients undergoing complex PCI are at risk of hypotension, decompensated heart failure, shock, or arrhythmias leading to rapid hemodynamic deterioration or death. Intra-aortic balloon pump counterpulsation offers minimal hemodynamic support but improves coronary and cerebral perfusion, with limitations in patients with peripheral artery or aortic disease. Impella left ventricular–assist devices provide greater support but are limited in those with left ventricular thrombus, stenosis, or vascular disease. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and Tandem-Heart devices are rarely used. Randomized trials (eg, PROTECT II) and observational studies have evaluated efficacy, safety, and cost, demonstrating mixed results and identifying select patients who may benefit.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for Hemodynamic Support in Complex PCI

rows.recommendation: In selected high-risk patients, elective insertion of an appropriate hemodynamic support device as an adjunct to PCI may be reasonable to prevent hemodynamic compromise during PCI (1,2).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Aspirin and Oral P2Y12 Inhibitors in Patients Undergoing PCI

rows.recommendation: In patients undergoing PCI, a loading dose of aspirin, followed by daily dosing, is recommended to reduce ischemic events (1-4).*
In patients with ACS undergoing PCI, a loading dose of P2Y12 inhibitor, followed by daily dosing, is recommended to reduce ischemic events (5-15).
In patients with SIHD undergoing PCI, a loading dose of clopidogrel, followed by daily dosing, is recommended to reduce ischemic events (8,12,15-19).
In patients undergoing PCI within 24 hours after fibrinolytic therapy, a loading dose of 300 mg of clopidogrel, followed by daily dosing, is recommended to reduce ischemic events (5).

content.narrative_summary: Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and oral P2Y12 inhibitors is the cornerstone of preventing thrombotic complications in patients undergoing PCI. rows.recommendation: 1. In patients undergoing PCI who are P2Y12 inhibitor naïve, intravenous cangrelor may be reasonable to reduce periprocedural ischemic events (1-3).
rows.supporting_text:
Recommendation-Specific Supporting Text:
1. The CHAMPION PLATFORM and the CHAMPION PCI trials did not show a reduction in the primary outcome (i.e., death, MI, or ischemia-driven revascularization at 48 hours) with cangrelor. However, in CHAMPION PLATFORM, cangrelor resulted in lower rates of the prespecified secondary outcomes of stent thrombosis and death (1). In the CHAMPION PHOENIX trial, the primary endpoint, which included death, MI, ischemia-driven revascularization, or stent thrombosis, was significantly reduced with cangrelor (2). This was driven mainly by a reduction in periprocedural MI and intraprocedural stent thrombosis. A pooled patient-level meta-analysis of the CHAMPION trials supported these findings, demonstrating a lower rate of the composite endpoint of death, MI, ischemia-driven revascularization, or stent thrombosis at 48 hours with cangrelor than with clopidogrel (3). Additionally, cangrelor was associated with a 41% reduction in stent thrombosis. Although major bleeding was similar between the groups, minor bleeding was more frequent in the cangrelor group (3).

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with ACS undergoing PCI with large thrombus burden, no-reflow, or slow flow, intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor agents are reasonable to improve procedural success (1,2).
2. In patients with SIHD undergoing PCI, the routine use of an intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor agent is not recommended (3-5).

section_headings: 12.1. Perioperative Considerations in Patients Undergoing CABG
content.narrative_summary: Previous perioperative management recommendations emphasized intraoperative and postoperative monitoring modalities and fast-track cardiac anesthesia to improve outcomes after CABG. Recent efforts have focused on multidisciplinary enhanced recovery programs incorporating bundled surgical, anesthetic, and nursing interventions—including targeted monitoring modalities—to optimize care, reduce opioid use, shorten extubation times, and decrease length of stay. Early data are from moderate-sized observational studies, and further research is needed to refine program components and implementation strategies outlined in Table 11.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis discusses selection of graft conduits for CABG, noting clinical and technical factors (e.g., life expectancy, diabetes, CKD, target stenosis) and supporting the use of the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) to graft the LAD for improved survival. rows.recommendation: In patients undergoing isolated CABG, the use of a radial artery is recommended in preference to a saphenous vein conduit to graft the second most important, significantly stenosed, non-LAD vessel to improve long-term cardiac outcomes (1-3).
In patients undergoing CABG, an IMA, preferably the left, should be used to bypass the LAD when bypass of the LAD is indicated to improve survival and reduce recurrent ischemic events (4-9).
In patients undergoing CABG, bilateral IMA (BIMA) grafting by experienced operators can be beneficial in appropriate patients to improve long-term cardiac outcomes (3,10-12).

section_headings: 12.3. CABG in Patients Undergoing Other Cardiac Surgery
content.narrative_summary: Registry data (CASS) and observational studies demonstrate that LIMA-LAD grafting reduces death, recurrent infarction, rehospitalization, and repeat revascularization, with higher long-term patency. Meta-analyses of BIMA use show decreased mortality at 7.5 years, although a large RCT found no difference in 10-year all-cause mortality. Higher institutional BIMA volume and protocol adherence are associated with improved outcomes, but sternal infection risk should be weighed during preoperative planning.

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients undergoing valve surgery, aortic surgery, or other cardiac operations who have significant CAD, CABG is recommended with a goal of reducing ischemic events (1–11).
2. In patients undergoing valve surgery, aortic surgery, or other cardiac operations who have intermediate CAD, CABG may be reasonable with a goal of reducing ischemic events (5,7,10,12).

content.narrative_summary: Sternal wound infection in CABG surgery is now reported at <1% but remains associated with significant mortality, morbidity, and cost. Management of perioperative hyperglycemia with continuous intravenous insulin infusion to maintain blood glucose <180 mg/dL reduces postoperative complications (mediastinitis, arrhythmias, wound infections, renal failure) and improves survival. Optimal intraoperative glycemic targets remain uncertain. Alongside standard antibiotic prophylaxis, additional strategies have emerged as best practices to further reduce sternal wound infection risk.

rows.recommendation: In patients undergoing CABG, the use of continuous intravenous insulin to achieve and maintain an early postoperative blood glucose concentration of <180 mg/dL while avoiding hypoglycemia is indicated to reduce the incidence of adverse events, including deep sternal wound infection (3–6).
In patients undergoing CABG, a comprehensive approach to reduce sternal wound infection is recommended (7–14).
In patients undergoing CABG, the usefulness of continuous intravenous insulin designed to achieve a target intraoperative blood glucose concentration <140 mg/dL is uncertain (4,15).

section_headings: 13.2. Antiplatelet Therapy in Patients Undergoing CABG
content.narrative_summary: The page includes a synopsis of the use of aspirin and antiplatelet agents in CABG patients, discussing assessment by the Heart Team, balancing myocardial ischemia risk versus bleeding and transfusion risks. It introduces recommendation-specific supporting text, beginning with observational data on preoperative aspirin use and reduced in-hospital mortality, before cutting off mid-discussion.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Antiplatelet Therapy in Patients Undergoing CABG

rows.recommendation: In patients undergoing CABG who are already taking daily aspirin preoperatively, it is recommended that they continue taking aspirin until the time of surgery to reduce ischemic events (1–7).
In patients referred for urgent CABG, clopidogrel and ticagrelor should be discontinued for at least 24 hours before surgery to reduce major bleeding complications (8–11).

In patients undergoing CABG, discontinuation of short-acting glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (eptifibatide and tirofiban) for 4 hours and abciximab for 12 hours before surgery is recommended to reduce the risk of bleeding and transfusion (12–14).

In patients undergoing elective CABG who receive P2Y12 receptor inhibitors before surgery, it is reasonable to discontinue clopidogrel for 5 days, ticagrelor for 3 days, and prasugrel for 7 days before CABG to reduce risk of major bleeding and blood product transfusion (8,9,11,15–23).

In patients undergoing elective CABG who are not already taking aspirin, the initiation of aspirin (100–300 mg daily) in the immediate preoperative period (<24 hours before surgery) is not recommended (24,25).

content.title: Beta Blockers and Amiodarone in Patients Undergoing CABG
section_headings: 13.3 Beta Blockers and Amiodarone in Patients Undergoing CABG
content.narrative_summary:
Continuation of recommendations regarding perioperative antiplatelet and anticoagulant management for CABG:  
• Aspirin continuation until surgery reduces MI risk but increases bleeding/transfusion without raising reoperation likelihood.  
• Coadministration of aspirin with P2Y12 inhibitors requires balancing ischemic versus bleeding risk when planning discontinuation before CABG.  
• Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors’ variable half-lives and renal function guide safe discontinuation timing prior to CABG.  
• Performing CABG <5 days after clopidogrel cessation increases major bleeding and tamponade risk; delaying surgery ≥72 hours for ticagrelor and similar windows for prasugrel likely reduces bleeding.  
• Immediate preoperative aspirin (<24 hours) yields no clear net benefit and may increase bleeding/transfusion.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Beta Blockers and Amiodarone in Patients Undergoing CABG

rows.recommendation: In patients undergoing CABG, who do not have a contraindication to beta blockers, the administration of beta blockers before surgery can be beneficial to reduce the incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation (1-8).
In patients undergoing CABG, preoperative amiodarone is reasonable to reduce the incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation (9-11).
In patients undergoing CABG, who do not have a contraindication to beta blockers, preoperative use of beta blockers may be effective in reducing in-hospital and 30-day mortality rates (12-18).
In patients undergoing CABG, the role of preoperative beta blockers for the prevention of acute postoperative myocardial ischemia, stroke, AKI, or ventricular arrhythmia is uncertain (12-14,18).

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of antiplatelet therapy after CABG, noting that bleeding risk is an important consideration. Older data have shown that aspirin improves vein graft patency and reduces ischemic complications. One small study demonstrated higher bleeding rates with aspirin post-CABG, but overall evidence supports early use of aspirin (1-6). Small RCTs, observational data, and meta-analyses demonstrate that DAPT (aspirin plus clopidogrel) after CABG improves vein graft patency, primarily in off-pump procedures. The DACAB trial compared DAPT with single antiplatelet therapy in 500 patients (75% off-pump); at 1-year follow-up, the DAPT group had the highest vein graft patency on CT angiography compared with aspirin alone.

content.narrative_summary: The first synopsis describes new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation after CABG, its incidence (~18%), associated risks (4-fold stroke, 3-fold all-cause mortality), and challenges in prevention and treatment, noting conflicting RCT results on beta-blocker perioperative use with no clear mortality or event benefit. The second synopsis reviews management of antiplatelet therapy in patients with atrial fibrillation undergoing PCI on anticoagulation, summarizing that trials (AUGUSTUS, ENTRUST-AF-PCI) showed lower bleeding with dual therapy (NOAC plus P2Y12 inhibitor) compared to triple therapy, prompting updated recommendations.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Antiplatelet Therapy in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation on Anticoagulation After PCI

rows.recommendation: In patients with atrial fibrillation who are undergoing PCI and are taking oral anticoagulant therapy, it is recommended to discontinue aspirin treatment after 1 to 4 weeks while maintaining P2Y12 inhibitors in addition to a non-vitamin K oral anticoagulant (rivaroxaban, dabigatran, apixaban, or edoxaban) or warfarin to reduce the risk of bleeding (1-7).

In patients with atrial fibrillation who are undergoing PCI, are taking oral anticoagulant therapy, and are treated with DAPT or a P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy, it is reasonable to choose a non-vitamin K oral anticoagulant over warfarin to reduce the risk of bleeding (1,3,4).

content.title: 15. Recommendations for Addressing Psychosocial Factors and Lifestyle Changes After Revascularization
section_headings: 15. Recommendations for Addressing Psychosocial Factors and Lifestyle Changes After Revascularization
content.narrative_summary: Cardiac rehabilitation is an evidence-based intervention comprising patient education, behavior modification, and exercise training to improve secondary prevention outcomes in patients with cardiovascular disease. It assists with adherence to healthy lifestyle habits, addresses comorbid conditions, monitors safety, and facilitates adherence to evidence-based medical therapies. Programs may be center-based with face-to-face supervised exercise or home-based models that meet safety and effectiveness criteria. Barriers such as transportation, competing demands, and program availability can impede participation. Cochrane reviews indicate similar quality-of-life and cost outcomes between home- and center-based programs. Recommendation-specific supportive text underscores: (1) the well-established safety and effectiveness of traditional, medically supervised center-based cardiac rehabilitation demonstrated by observational studies and RCTs in reducing hospital readmissions, secondary events, and mortality; and (2) the importance of providing patients and caregivers comprehensive care plans and educational materials during hospitalization to support adherence to evidence-based therapies, tailored by age, health literacy, cultural practices, and socioeconomic status, as captured in programs like AHA’s Life’s Simple 7.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Cardiac Rehabilitation and Education

rows.recommendation: In patients who have undergone revascularization, a comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation program (home based or center based) should be prescribed either before hospital discharge or during the first outpatient visit to reduce deaths and hospital readmissions and improve quality of life (1–4).
Patients who have undergone revascularization should be educated about CVD risk factors and their modification to reduce cardiovascular events (5–7).

content.title: 15.2. Smoking Cessation in Patients After Revascularization
content.narrative_summary: Tobacco use, especially cigarette smoking, is a leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality; continued smoking after coronary revascularization is linked to adverse outcomes including stent thrombosis. Electronic nicotine delivery systems (e-cigarettes) emit particulates and toxic gases that may increase cardiovascular risk. Hospitalization after revascularization presents a timely opportunity for smoking cessation counseling. Varenicline and bupropion, combined with behavioral support, are effective and safe first-line pharmacotherapies, and supportive follow-up for at least one month post-discharge further increases abstinence rates.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Smoking Cessation in Patients After Revascularization

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients who use tobacco and have undergone coronary revascularization, a combination of behavioral interventions plus pharmacotherapy is recommended to maximize cessation and reduce adverse cardiac events (1–3).

2. In patients who use tobacco and have undergone coronary revascularization, smoking cessation interventions are recommended during hospitalization and should include supportive follow-up for at least 1 month after discharge to facilitate tobacco cessation and reduce morbidity and mortality (4–6).

content.title: 15.3. Psychological Interventions in Patients After Revascularization
content.narrative_summary: The page discusses the psychosocial morbidity associated with cardiac events and coronary revascularization, highlighting anxiety, depression, and stress as independent risk factors for poor adherence, quality of life, health care costs, and recurrent cardiac events. It notes pre- and postoperative depression rates in CABG patients and describes psychological therapies—relaxation, stress management, coping skills, and cognitive behavioral therapy—used in cardiac rehabilitation. The recommendation-specific supportive text summarizes trial evidence: EsDEPACS (escitalopram reducing depression and long-term MACE/MI risk), ENRICHD (counseling/SSRI improving depression but not survival), a subgroup analysis showing 42% lower risk of death/MI with SSRI, the Bypassing the Blues trial (collaborative care reducing depression scores and improving quality of life), and meta-analyses. It also reviews observational data and society recommendations for depression screening post-ACS, and the CODIACS-QoL trial showing no overall benefit of universal screening.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Psychological Interventions in Patients After Revascularization — Referenced studies that support the recommendations are summarized in Online Data Supplement 51

rows.recommendation: In patients who have undergone coronary revascularization who have symptoms of depression, anxiety, or stress, treatment with cognitive behavioral therapy, psychological counseling, and/or pharmacological interventions is beneficial to improve quality of life and cardiac outcomes (1-7).
In patients who have undergone coronary revascularization, it may be reasonable to screen for depression and refer or treat when it is indicated to improve quality of life and recovery (8,9).

section_headings: 16.1. Assessment of Outcomes in Patients After Revascularization
content.narrative_summary: This section introduces recommendations for assessment of outcomes in patients after revascularization, noting that referenced studies supporting the recommendations are summarized in Online Data Supplement 52.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Assessment of Outcomes in Patients After Revascularization

rows.recommendation: With the goal of improving patient outcomes, it is recommended that cardiac surgery and PCI programs participate in state, regional, or national clinical data registries and receive periodic reports of their risk-adjusted outcomes as a quality assessment and improvement strategy.

With the goal of improving patient outcomes, it is reasonable for cardiac surgery and PCI programs to have a quality improvement program that routinely 1) reviews institutional quality programs and outcomes, 2) reviews individual operator outcomes, 3) provides peer review of difficult or complicated cases, and 4) performs random case reviews.
Smaller volume cardiac surgery and PCI programs may consider affiliating with a high-volume center to improve patient care.

content.narrative_summary:
Synopsis: Centers performing coronary revascularization should engage in regional, state, or national risk-adjusted registries to benchmark performance, identify areas for improvement, and disseminate best practices. Quality and performance measures—spanning structure, processes, and outcomes—enable more reliable assessment than institutional- or operator-level volumes alone. Smaller or lower-volume programs benefit from affiliation, standardized processes, and peer collaboration, including staff exchanges and videoconferenced teaching.

Section 17: Unanswered Questions and Future Directions: Indications for revascularization are primarily derived from randomized trials and observational registries or patient cohorts showing outcome trends. Persistent sex, racial, and ethnic disparities in care and outcomes warrant efforts to enroll underrepresented groups in clinical trials. In patients with left ventricular dysfunction, CABG improves survival compared with medical therapy; however, the role of myocardial viability testing in guiding revascularization remains unclear.

section_headings: 17.2.6 Antiplatelet Therapy in Patients With ACS After CABG With an Indication for Anticoagulation
17.3.1 Use of the Radial Artery for a Conduit After Radial Artery Catheterization
content.narrative_summary: Section 17.2.2 discusses spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) as a cause of ACS in young women, noting conservative management is often preferred and further study is needed to define optimal revascularization techniques. Section 17.2.3 reviews coronary artery aneurysms and fistulas, emphasizing their rarity, varied repair methods, and lack of randomized evidence to guide timing of intervention. Section 17.2.4 describes myocardial bridging, its prevalence, potential clinical significance, diagnostic strategies (including FFR and imaging under stress), and uncertainty regarding long-term outcomes of surgical versus percutaneous treatment. Section 17.2.5 reports sparse data on managing arterial graft failure after CABG and recommends Heart Team discussion for percutaneous interventions. Section 17.2.6 notes absence of data to guide antiplatelet therapy in ACS patients on anticoagulation following CABG and highlights need for individualized assessment of bleeding and thromboembolic risks. Section 17.3 introduces general revascularization considerations, and 17.3.1 begins to outline the increasing use of the radial artery as a bypass conduit after radial catheterization.
